2051.title: Team Autonomy
2051.heading: Team Autonomy
2051.content: Team autonomy is the ability to deliver changes within an owned business capability without waiting continually for other teams. It improves when a cross-functional team owns complete [[Bounded Context]]s rather than one technical layer shared by every feature. Autonomy does not eliminate alignment: teams still agree on outcomes and boundary contracts. It reduces coordination queues, context switching, and unfinished work, supporting [[Loose Coupling and High Alignment]] at the organizational level.

2054.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
2054.heading: TCP Three-Way Handshake
2054.content:
The TCP three-way handshake establishes shared connection state before application data is transferred. A client requests synchronization, the server acknowledges and supplies its own synchronization value, and the client acknowledges the server's response.

This exchange confirms that both endpoints can send and receive and establishes the sequence information used for ordered delivery. It adds a setup round trip that a connectionless protocol does not require.

2057.title: TCP IP
2057.heading: TCP IP
2057.content:
TCP/IP is the protocol suite that connects heterogeneous networks into the Internet. TCP manages reliable end-to-end data exchange, while IP addresses and routes individual packets across intervening networks.

Separating these responsibilities lets local networks use different technologies while presenting a common internetwork service. The suite has remained the Internet’s technical foundation since ARPANET adopted it.

2060.title: Taylor Series
2060.heading: Taylor Series
2060.content:
A Taylor series represents a sufficiently differentiable function near a point using its derivatives there. Truncating the series produces a polynomial approximation whose remainder measures the omitted higher-order behavior.

First-order terms provide a local linear approximation. Second-order terms introduce the [[Hessian Matrix]] for multivariable functions and motivate Newton-type optimization and root-finding methods.

2063.title: Tautology
2063.heading: Tautology
2063.content:
A tautology is a [[Compound Propositions|compound proposition]] that is true under every possible assignment of truth values to its variables. A contradiction is false under every assignment.

Two propositions are [[Logically Equivalent]] exactly when their biconditional is a tautology. Tautologies therefore express laws of logic that remain valid regardless of what the component propositions mean.

2066.title: Task Continuation
2066.heading: Task Continuation
2066.content:
A task continuation schedules work that depends on an earlier task's completion. It can inspect the antecedent's result, cancellation, or exception and can be configured to run only under selected completion conditions.

Continuations expose the dependency graph directly, but long chains can become difficult to read and reason about. For naturally asynchronous workflows, C# `async` and `await` usually express the same sequencing with clearer control flow and exception handling.

2069.title: Task Card
2069.heading: Task Card
2069.content:
A task card records a concrete piece of work needed to implement a backlog item. Cards are created and revised by the team during [[Sprint Planning]] and development, then moved across a visible board as their state changes.

A card is a coordination aid, not proof of product value. Progress is ultimately judged by completed backlog items and the integrated [[Product Increment]].

2072.title: Task Analysis
2072.heading: Task Analysis
2072.content:
Task analysis identifies the tasks and subtasks people perform and describes their relationships, sequences, and dependencies. A hierarchical task analysis arranges them into a structure that exposes how a larger activity is completed.

The result helps derive requirements and choose appropriate [[Interaction Technique]]s. For example, treating all [[3D Manipulation]] as one task hides important differences among selection, positioning, rotation, and scaling. Breaking the work into canonical tasks and task parameters makes design and evaluation more precise.

Task analysis supports [[Requirements Analysis]], [[User-Centered Design]], and application-specific [[User Interface Evaluation]].

2075.heading: Target Viewpoint Guidance
2075.content:
Target viewpoint guidance helps a user reproduce a required camera or observer pose rather than merely locate an object. The interface compares the current position and orientation with the target view and shows how to reduce the difference.

This is useful when an inspection, photograph, reconstruction, or comparison depends on seeing the scene from a particular perspective. Position and orientation errors need cues that the user can act on separately.

2078.heading: Target Object Guidance
2078.content:
Target object guidance directs a user toward a physical or augmented object that is not currently visible. The interface communicates direction and sometimes distance while preserving awareness of the surrounding environment.

Once the object enters view, registered highlighting or annotation can replace the off-screen cue. The transition should make clear that both cues refer to the same target and avoid directing attention through an unsafe or impossible route.

2081.heading: Target Hardware Polygon Budget
2081.content:
A polygon budget allocates geometric complexity according to the devices expected to run the game. Mobile hardware, older computers, and high-end desktops cannot display the same scene cost at the same frame rate.

The budget applies to the whole visible scene, not each object in isolation. Prominent interactive assets may receive more geometry while distant or repeated objects rely on simpler meshes, [[Baked Surface Detail for Low-Poly Assets|baked detail]], and level-of-detail variants.

2084.title: Target Audience
2084.heading: Target Audience
2084.content:
A target audience is the group for whom a game is intentionally designed. It is best described through motivations, preferences, experience, and play context, with demographics included only when they matter to the design.

“Everyone” is not a useful target because players have different skills and [[Interactivity Budget|interactivity budgets]]. Audience assumptions shape game scope, complexity, presentation, and which forms of [[Player Motivation]] the experience supports.

2087.sourceSearchName: target audience playtest target audience playtest

2087.heading: Target Audience Playtest
2087.content:
A target-audience playtest recruits people who are likely to seek the intended kind of experience. It asks whether a sufficiently developed prototype fulfills its promise for the players the project means to serve.

This test becomes useful after the core experience exists; using it too early can make participants evaluate missing finish instead of the design question. Audience fit supplies evidence without turning majority preference into the game's creative direction.

2093.title: Tanh Activation Function
2093.heading: Tanh Activation Function
2093.content:
The tanh activation function is the hyperbolic tangent used as a neural activation. It has an S shape like the [[Sigmoid Activation Function]], but its output ranges from negative one to one.

Large negative input approaches negative one, zero maps to zero, and large positive input approaches one. Its negative outputs can represent an inhibitory effect while retaining a smooth function suitable for derivative-based training.

2096.sourceSearchName: tangible user interface tangible user interface
2096.title: Tangible User Interface
2096.heading: Tangible User Interface
2096.content:
A tangible user interface uses physical objects to represent digital information and to provide mechanisms for interacting with it. Computation can be distributed among objects that are aware of their location or proximity to other objects.

Because the physical representation and the control are integrated, users can apply existing skills for handling real-world objects. Multiple spatially aware objects can also support concurrent access and manipulation.

Tangible interfaces are a form of [[Embodied Interaction]] and can overlap with [[Augmented Reality]] when physical objects are enhanced by digital information.

In AR, tangibles may have generic shapes whose tracked pose controls virtual content or distinctive shapes whose physical form identifies their role. The object supplies grasping, contact, and shared-space cues, while augmentation adds changeable appearance and behavior that the physical artifact cannot provide alone.

2099.sourceSearchName: tangent line approximation tangent line approximation
2099.title: Tangent Line Approximation
2099.heading: Tangent Line Approximation
2099.content:
Near a differentiable point $x=a$, a function is approximated by its tangent line

$$f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).$$

The derivative supplies the slope of the best local linear approximation. The error shrinks faster than the horizontal displacement as $x$ approaches $a$, distinguishing tangency from merely passing through the same point.

2108.title: Tacit Knowledge Challenge to AI
2108.heading: Tacit Knowledge Challenge to AI
2108.content:
The tacit knowledge challenge to AI holds that much intelligent behavior relies on practical know-how that people cannot fully state as explicit rules. Everyday action depends on recognizing what matters in a situation against a background of embodied experience and social practice.

This creates a problem for systems that assume intelligence can be captured by formal representations alone: every rule requires relevance conditions that may themselves need more rules. Data-driven systems can learn patterns without hand-coding every instruction, but learned correlation does not automatically provide human meaning or situated judgment. The challenge therefore remains relevant to both symbolic and statistical AI.

2117.title: t-Distribution
2117.heading: t-Distribution
2117.content:
The t-distribution describes a standardized sample mean when the population is normal but its variance is estimated from the same sample. It has heavier tails than the normal distribution because the denominator contains additional sampling uncertainty.

Degrees of freedom control the tail thickness. As sample size grows, the variance estimate stabilizes and the t-distribution approaches the normal distribution used by the [[Central Limit Theorem]].

2120.title: Syzygy
2120.heading: Syzygy
2120.content:
A syzygy is a relation among generators f₁,…,fₜ of a module: a tuple (r₁,…,rₜ) such that r₁f₁ + ··· + rₜfₜ = 0.

All first syzygies form the [[Syzygy Module]]. Repeating the construction on generators of that module produces higher syzygies and the successive kernels in a free resolution.

2123.title: Syzygy Module
2123.heading: Syzygy Module
2123.content:
The syzygy module Syz(f₁,…,fₜ) is the submodule of Rᵗ containing every [[Syzygy]] among the listed generators. It is the kernel of the map Rᵗ → M that sends standard basis vectors to those generators.

Generators of this kernel become columns of a [[Presentation Matrix]]. Higher syzygy modules continue the relations-among-relations structure of a free resolution.

2126.title: Systems Thinking
2126.heading: Systems Thinking
2126.content:
Systems thinking studies both the parts of a system and the unified behavior created by their interactions. It combines the analytic strengths of [[Reductionism]] with the whole-oriented view of [[Holism]].

The method moves repeatedly among [[System State|state]], [[System Behavior|behavior]], interaction loops, the resulting whole, and its wider context. This makes it especially useful for designing a [[Complex System]], where feedback and [[Emergence]] make isolated parts an incomplete explanation.

In an organization, systems thinking shifts improvement from individual utilization to the flow of value, information, and decisions across teams. It reveals how structure and communication can shape both development behavior and the architecture of the product.

2129.title: Systemic Reward
2129.heading: Systemic Reward
2129.content:
A systemic reward feeds back into the playable system by enabling new actions or opportunities. It may grant a new [[Game Verb]], provide a [[Resource]], reveal new objects, or unlock a new area.

Because it changes what the player can do next, a systemic reward connects past accomplishment to future play. It differs from a [[Dead-End Reward]], which may be pleasurable but does not alter the system being played.

2132.title: Systemic Model
2132.heading: Systemic Model
2132.content:
A systemic model represents parts, their internal state, and the interactions that form feedback loops. It exposes how aggregate behavior is produced rather than describing only an input-output equation.

Like a mathematical model, it is an abstraction rather than a complete copy of reality. Its value lies in choosing a [[System Boundary]] and level of detail that reveal the dynamics relevant to the design question.

2134.title: Systemic Elegance
2134.heading: Document
2134.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Emergent Systems]] [[Game Mechanics and Rules]]

2135.title: Systemic Elegance
2135.heading: Systemic Elegance
2135.content:
Systemic elegance is the creation of rich, persistent behavior from a small set of consistent rules and few exceptions. It combines a simple high-level structure with [[Systemic Depth]] and recurring patterns across levels.

Consistency reduces [[Cognitive Load]] and helps a player transfer learning between subsystems. An elegant system is therefore approachable while still producing a broad [[Play Space]] that remains difficult to exhaust or master.

Elegance also depends on a concise interactive vocabulary. Underdeveloped verbs and objects occupy the player's attention without adding comparable depth, while a smaller set of robust elements can support discovery through many relationships.

2138.title: Systemic Game
2138.heading: Systemic Game
2138.content:
A systemic game derives much of its gameplay from interacting feedback loops rather than from a single authored sequence. The systems generate a [[Play Space]] in which players can pursue many paths and produce emergent outcomes.

Systemic structure supports replayability and mastery because the same parts can combine differently across play. It does not eliminate content; it uses content as material within systems rather than relying on a continuous [[Content-Driven Game|content treadmill]].

When relationships among verbs and objects create many possible situations, players can discover strategies and produce [[Emergent Story|stories]] the creator did not script. The system still bounds those outcomes, but it facilitates rather than fully authors their sequence.

2140.sourceSearchName: systemic game design systemic game design
2140.title: Systemic Game Design
2140.heading: Document

2141.sourceSearchName: systemic game design systemic game design
2141.title: Systemic Game Design
2141.heading: Systemic Game Design
2141.content:
Systemic game design creates a desired player experience by moving among the whole, the feedback loops that produce it, and the parts that implement those loops. It uses [[Systems Thinking]] to decompose and recompose the game without losing either level.

The designer directly specifies parts and relationships, then iterates through prototypes and playtests to observe the emergent [[Game-Player System]]. This makes design a [[Designer Loop]] rather than a one-pass act of specification.

2142.sourceSearchName: systemic game design systemic game design
2142.title: Systemic Game Design
2142.heading: References

2144.title: Systemic Depth
2144.heading: Systemic Depth
2144.content:
Systemic depth is the presence of multiple meaningful levels of interacting subsystems within a design. It comes from nested loops and production chains rather than simply adding unrelated features.

Depth expands possible relationships while recurring structures can scaffold learning from one level to the next. This can make a game difficult to master without making it needlessly difficult to learn, an aspect of [[Systemic Elegance]].

2147.title: System
2147.heading: System
2147.content:
A system is a set of parts whose interactions form loops that create a persistent whole. The whole has properties and behaviors that do not belong to any single part and are not merely the parts added together.

Each part has [[System State|state]], a [[System Boundary|boundary]], and [[System Behavior|behaviors]]. A system may also be a part inside a larger [[System Hierarchy]], so the appropriate boundary depends on the behavior being studied.

2149.title: Systematic Error
2149.heading: Document
2149.content:
2026-09-17 00:04

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Physical Measurement and Experimental Analysis]]

2150.title: Systematic Error
2150.heading: Systematic Error
2150.content: Systematic error biases measurements consistently because of calibration, procedure, or an unrecognized environmental effect. Repeating the same method does not remove it and may produce a tightly clustered but inaccurate result. Detection requires independent calibration, altered methods, or comparison with an external standard rather than averaging alone.

2153.title: System State
2153.heading: System State
2153.content:
System state is the aggregate of the current values of a system's attributes. It describes the system at a particular moment, such as the amount of a resource in a [[Stock]] or the health of a game character.

State changes over time through [[System Behavior|behaviors]] and interactions. Because later actions depend on current state, feedback loops make the history of changes consequential to future behavior.

2156.title: System Source
2156.heading: System Source
2156.content:
A system source generates a [[Resource]] or increases the amount available to another part. The source may represent a concrete origin, such as a mine, or an abstract event, such as receiving experience for an action.

A model can treat the resource as appearing from outside its [[System Boundary]] when representing the larger origin would add detail without useful behavior. Excess source flow without adequate [[System Sink|sinks]] can create [[Economic Inflation]].

2159.title: System Sink
2159.heading: System Sink
2159.content:
A system sink removes a [[Resource]] from the modeled system. What happens afterward lies beyond the chosen [[System Boundary]], so a sink is sometimes also called a drain.

Sinks regulate resource accumulation and are essential to many [[Balancing Loop|balancing loops]]. Too few sinks can produce [[Economic Inflation]], while sinks that drain too aggressively can contribute to [[Economic Stagnation]].

2161.sourceSearchName: system integrity verification system integrity verification
2161.title: System Integrity Verification
2161.heading: Document

2162.sourceSearchName: system integrity verification system integrity verification
2162.title: System Integrity Verification
2162.heading: System Integrity Verification
2162.content:
System integrity verification provides evidence that a computer has not been altered or compromised since a trusted state. The source combines user identity verification, secure boot, and hashing of files, folders, or an entire drive to examine different layers of the host.

The order matters: data checks are less meaningful when the operating system performing them cannot be trusted. A verified host provides the foundation on which [[Data Integrity Verification]] can rely.

2163.title: System Integrity Verification

2164.sourceSearchName: system of parameters system of parameters
2164.title: System of Parameters
2164.heading: Document

2165.sourceSearchName: system of parameters system of parameters
2165.title: System of Parameters
2165.heading: System of Parameters
2165.content:
For a finitely generated module M over a Noetherian local ring, a system of parameters is a set a₁,…,aₙ in the maximal ideal such that M/(a₁,…,aₙ)M has finite [[Module Length]].

A minimal system has length equal to the [[Dimension of a Module]]. In a [[Regular Local Ring]], a system of parameters that generates the maximal ideal is a regular system of parameters.

2166.sourceSearchName: system of parameters system of parameters
2166.title: System of Parameters
2166.heading: References

2168.title: System Boundary
2168.heading: System Boundary
2168.content:
A system boundary distinguishes the parts included in a system from its environment. In a complex system, the boundary is often recognized through a dense cluster of local interactions rather than imposed as an arbitrary line.

A practical test is whether something can materially change the behavior of the whole: if it can, it may belong inside the boundary under study. Because systems are nested in a [[System Hierarchy]], a useful boundary changes with the level and question being examined.

2171.title: System Hierarchy
2171.heading: System Hierarchy
2171.content:
A system hierarchy is an organization in which a system contains lower-level systems as parts and is itself a part of a higher-level system. Each level has behaviors that can be described without reproducing every detail below it.

Designers move among these integrative levels to connect atomic parts, loops, and the complete experience. Clear levels support [[Systemic Depth]], while long nonlocal dependencies across levels can make a design brittle.

2174.title: System Control
2174.heading: System Control
2174.content:
System control is the task of issuing commands that request a function, change the interaction mode, or change system state. The user specifies what should happen and leaves the details of execution to the system.

System control connects other tasks such as [[Object Selection]], [[3D Manipulation]], and [[3D Travel]]. It can use physical controllers, graphical menus, voice, gestures, tools, or [[Multimodal Interaction]].

Good system control preserves the flow of action, limits focus and device switching, exposes available commands, organizes functions clearly, and provides unmistakable [[Feedback]] about the current mode. A 2D or hybrid control can be preferable even inside a [[3D User Interface]].

2177.title: System Behavior
2177.heading: System Behavior
2177.content:
System behavior is an action by which a part changes its own state, affects another part, or communicates a resource or message. Behaviors are the active connections that turn a collection of parts into loops.

One part can perturb another, but the receiving part determines its own response. Keeping that response local supports encapsulation, [[Modular Behavior]], and the possibility of [[Emergence]].

2179.title: Synthetic Media
2179.heading: Document

Tags: [[Data Ethics and Digital Power]], [[Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics]]
links: Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics

2180.title: Synthetic Media
2180.heading: Synthetic Media
2180.content:
Synthetic media are images, audio, video, or text generated or altered so that fabricated content can appear authentic. AI lowers the effort required to imitate people, invent events, and automate persuasive communication.

The ethical harm includes more than a single deception. When fabricated media become common, genuine evidence can also be dismissed as fake, weakening trust in communication and public institutions. Bots can amplify the effect by simulating social agreement or overwhelming discussion. Disclosure of artificial identity and methods for verification help, but the broader problem concerns the social conditions under which people decide what to believe.

From a forensic perspective, computer-generated faces and scenes may omit traces of physical image formation, including camera-sensor correlations or subtle physiological signals. Machine-learning systems can rapidly improve after a detector becomes known, so these artifacts are evidence about a particular generation pipeline rather than permanent proof that all synthetic media will share the same flaw.
links: Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics

2183.title: Synthesis Flow
2183.heading: Synthesis Flow
2183.content:
A synthesis flow turns an accelerator description into implementable hardware through analysis, scheduling, logic generation, placement, routing, and verification. Reports estimate timing, area, memory use, and achievable frequency before deployment.

Iteration is essential because an algorithmically correct design may miss performance or resource goals once interfaces and physical constraints are included.

2186.title: Synchronous Play
2186.heading: Synchronous Play
2186.content:
Synchronous play requires participants to be connected during the same period. Actions may be real-time or turn-based, but each player's progress depends on the others being present.

The design must handle waiting, late arrival, and sudden absence. Session length and scheduling become part of accessibility because participation requires overlapping time.

2188.title: Syntax Analysis
2188.heading: Document

2026-09-18 17:13

2189.title: Syntax Analysis
2189.heading: Syntax Analysis
2189.content:
Syntax analysis checks whether a token sequence follows the grammar of a language and organizes valid tokens into a structural representation. The parser recognizes expressions, statements, blocks, and other constructs after [[Lexical Analysis]] has identified their tokens.

The resulting tree or intermediate form can be interpreted or converted into instructions for a [[Script Virtual Machine]]. Syntax errors should identify the unexpected token and useful source context.

2192.title: Synchronous Messaging
2192.heading: Synchronous Messaging
2192.content:
Synchronous messaging makes a sender wait for reception or processing before it proceeds with dependent work. The communication therefore blocks one participant until the required interaction completes.

This provides a simple visible sequence but couples availability and response time: a slow or unavailable receiver delays the sender. [[Asynchronous Messaging]] removes that immediate wait by letting a queue hold the message for later retrieval.

2194.sourceSearchName: synchronized map views synchronized map views
2194.title: Synchronized Map Views
2194.heading: Document

2195.sourceSearchName: synchronized map views synchronized map views
2195.title: Synchronized Map Views
2195.heading: Synchronized Map Views
2195.content: Synchronized map views display related datasets in separate maps while sharing pan, zoom, and possibly cursor position. They let viewers compare spatial patterns without combining every layer into one obscured overlay. Each view should use compatible extents and clearly labeled legends, especially when scales differ. Linked navigation preserves geographic correspondence, but visual comparison still depends on consistent projections and panel sizes.

2198.heading: Symmetry Reduction in Thermal Geometry
2198.content:
Geometric symmetry can reduce a model to a fraction of the physical object when temperature and heat flux repeat across the omitted sectors. A symmetry boundary prevents normal heat flow across the cut plane and represents the mirrored continuation of the domain.

The reduction is invalid if an asymmetric source, material, flow, or boundary condition breaks the repeated pattern. When applicable, it permits finer [[Thermal Mesh Refinement|local resolution]] or shorter solution time without discarding distinct physical behavior.

2201.title: Symmetric-Key Rekeying
2201.heading: Symmetric-Key Rekeying
2201.content:
Symmetric-key rekeying replaces a shared encryption or authentication key according to an agreed update process. Regular change limits the amount of data exposed if one key is compromised and can support stream-by-stream verification.

Resource-constrained sensing systems need updates that are faster than public-key operations while remaining synchronized and resistant to lost, replayed, or reordered messages.

2204.title: Symmetric Matrix
2204.heading: Symmetric Matrix
2204.content:
A real square matrix is symmetric when $A^T=A$. Its entries mirror across the main diagonal.

Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and admit an orthonormal set of eigenvectors, enabling [[Orthogonal Diagonalization]]. They also arise as [[Hessian Matrix|Hessian matrices]], normal-equation matrices, and positive-definite coefficient matrices.

2207.title: Symmetric Group
2207.heading: Symmetric Group
2207.content:
The symmetric group Sₙ contains every permutation of an n-element set. It has n! elements and is generally nonabelian for n at least three.

Cycle structure, transpositions, and parity reveal important subgroups and generators of Sₙ.

2209.sourceSearchName: symmetric distance matrix cache symmetric distance matrix cache
2209.title: Symmetric Distance Matrix Cache
2209.heading: Document

2210.sourceSearchName: symmetric distance matrix cache symmetric distance matrix cache
2210.title: Symmetric Distance Matrix Cache
2210.heading: Symmetric Distance Matrix Cache
2210.content:
A symmetric distance matrix cache stores each pairwise value once under an unordered or normalized pair of record or cluster identifiers. Agglomerative methods consult and update this structure repeatedly as clusters merge.

Avoiding duplicate calculations nearly halves storage relative to a full directed map and removes redundant distance calls. Insertion, lookup, and deletion rules must consistently treat the two key orders as the same pair.

2211.title: Symmetric Distance Matrix Cache
2211.heading: References

2213.title: Symmetric Game
2213.heading: Symmetric Game
2213.content:
A symmetric game gives players the same starting conditions, goals, and rules. Symmetry makes fairness easier to establish because structural advantages are minimized.

Equal structure does not guarantee an interesting or perfectly even match: position, chance, and skill still matter. It provides a clear baseline from which remaining advantages can be examined.

2215.title: Symmetric Encryption
2215.heading: Document
2215.content:
2026-09-08 21:16

Status: #baby

Tags: [[.NET Cryptography and Access Control]] [[Applied Cryptography and PKI]]

2216.title: Symmetric Encryption
2216.heading: Symmetric Encryption
2216.content:
Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt plaintext and decrypt ciphertext. It is efficient for protecting substantial amounts of data, but every party that needs access must securely obtain and protect the shared key.

Confidentiality alone does not prove that encrypted data was not modified. A complete design must use an authenticated construction or pair encryption with appropriate integrity protection, while keeping keys separate from the data they protect.

Symmetric algorithms are comparatively fast and efficient for large volumes of data. Their main operational challenge is distributing the shared secret without exposing it, so secure protocols can use [[Asymmetric Encryption]] to protect the symmetric session key.

2219.heading: Symmetric Algebra of an Ideal
2219.content:
The symmetric algebra Sym(I) is the graded algebra generated formally by the elements of an ideal I, subject to the linear relations among those generators. It maps naturally onto the [[Rees Algebra]].

The Rees algebra also enforces nonlinear relations coming from actual products in I. When the natural map is an isomorphism, I is an [[Ideal of Linear Type]].

2222.title: Symbolic Inference
2222.heading: Symbolic Inference
2222.content:
Symbolic inference manipulates probability expressions before assigning numerical values. It applies identities such as normalization, factorization, and marginalization to simplify a Bayesian question algebraically.

The result may be a closed form or a smaller expression for later numerical evaluation. Symbolic work is especially valuable when the same model form will be queried repeatedly with different parameter values.

2225.sourceSearchName: symbol range grading symbol range grading
2225.title: Symbol Range Grading
2225.heading: Symbol Range Grading
2225.content: Symbol range grading selects a finite sequence of symbol sizes intended to be visually distinguishable across a [[Graduated Symbol Map]]. The data range is first divided into classes, then each class receives a representative size. Too many grades make neighboring symbols hard to tell apart, while too few conceal variation. Size selection must also account for map density so large symbols do not cover nearby locations.

2228.title: Symbol Area Scaling
2228.heading: Symbol Area Scaling
2228.content: Symbol area scaling makes a map symbol's area, rather than its radius, directly proportional to a data value. For circles this means radius grows with the square root of the value. Scaling radius directly would make area grow quadratically and greatly exaggerate large observations. Correct mathematical scaling establishes an honest geometric mapping, although [[Perceptual Symbol Scaling]] may still be considered because viewers tend to underestimate area differences.

2231.title: Sylvester Matrix
2231.heading: Sylvester Matrix
2231.content:
The Sylvester matrix of two positive-degree one-variable polynomials is formed by shifted rows of their coefficients. Its size is the sum of their degrees.

The determinant of this matrix is the [[Polynomial Resultant]]. A zero determinant means the coefficient equations admit a nontrivial relation, which occurs exactly when the two polynomials share a common factor.

2234.title: Sylow Theorem
2234.heading: Sylow Theorem
2234.content:
The Sylow theorems describe subgroups whose orders are the largest powers of a prime dividing a finite group order. They guarantee existence and constrain conjugacy and the possible number of such subgroups.

These constraints help determine group structure from its order.

2237.title: Sybil Attack
2237.heading: Sybil Attack
2237.content:
A Sybil attack occurs when one adversary creates or controls many apparently independent identities. The identities can distort voting, popularity, recommendation, reputation, or routing systems that assume each account represents a separate participant.

Defenses use stronger identity costs, social-graph structure, behavioral similarity, resource tests, and rate limits, but each technique trades openness and privacy against resistance to fake identities.

2240.title: SWIFT Bioprinting
2240.heading: SWIFT Bioprinting
2240.content:
Sacrificial writing into functional tissue, or SWIFT, prints a removable ink inside a dense cell-and-matrix support material. Removing the ink leaves hollow channels through which culture medium can be perfused.

The method addresses the oxygen and nutrient limits of thick constructs by building a vascular-like transport network into the living tissue.

2242.title: Sustainable AI
2242.heading: Document
2242.content:

Status: #baby

2243.title: Sustainable AI
2243.heading: Sustainable AI
2243.content:
Sustainable AI develops and uses artificial intelligence in ways compatible with long-term social and environmental well-being. It includes using AI to understand environmental systems while also reducing the energy, materials, waste, and unequal burdens created by AI itself.

The goal requires life-cycle thinking. A system is not sustainable merely because its application has an environmental purpose; production, infrastructure, and rebound effects still matter. Sustainability also includes human autonomy and justice, since an efficient solution that imposes authoritarian control or transfers pollution to vulnerable communities does not resolve the larger ethical problem.

2246.heading: Swept Sphere Collision
2246.content:
Swept sphere collision tests a sphere as it moves along a segment, producing the volume of a capsule-like sweep. Solving the resulting intersection can reveal whether and when another object enters that path.

Because it examines the space between frame positions, the technique catches impacts missed by [[Instantaneous Collision Detection]]. The earliest valid time in the update interval identifies the first contact.

The format established a workflow later extended by tools such as knitr.

The susceptible-infected-susceptible model allows an active node to stop transmitting and become susceptible again. Unlike the recovered state in an SIR process, the node can later be reinfected.

This recurrence changes the relationship between a current snapshot and its source because nodes may enter the active set more than once. Source estimation must use a model consistent with that possibility.

2255.heading: Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Model
2255.content:
The susceptible-infected-recovered model divides nodes into those not yet reached, those actively transmitting, and those informed but no longer transmitting. Infection and recovery probabilities govern movement between the three states.

For social information, an infected user is ready to pass the message and a recovered user has stopped forwarding it. The recovery state prevents a node from becoming active again in the basic model.

2258.title: Survival Probability
2258.heading: Survival Probability
2258.content:
Survival probability is the probability of remaining free of the event beyond a specified time. It decreases as events occur and is estimated while accounting for censored observations that leave the risk set.

It differs from simply subtracting overall event prevalence from one. At each event time, the calculation conditions on those still at risk, so both the numerator and denominator evolve throughout follow-up.

2260.sourceSearchName: survival model distribution selection survival model distribution selection
2260.title: Survival Model Distribution Selection
2260.heading: Document

2261.sourceSearchName: survival model distribution selection survival model distribution selection
2261.title: Survival Model Distribution Selection
2261.heading: Survival Model Distribution Selection
2261.content:
Survival model distribution selection compares the observed event-time experience with plausible parametric curves and considers whether a semiparametric Cox model is more defensible. Visual overlays, AIC, and hazard diagnostics provide complementary evidence.

The choice can materially change coefficient direction and interpretation. When reasonable distributions disagree or event times are unreliable, analysts should treat the instability as evidence about the limits of the analysis rather than select the preferred conclusion.

2262.sourceSearchName: survival model distribution selection survival model distribution selection
2262.title: Survival Model Distribution Selection
2262.heading: References

2264.title: Survival Curve
2264.heading: Survival Curve
2264.content:
A survival curve plots estimated survival probability against time. Its downward steps occur at observed events, while censored observations reduce the later risk set without directly causing a probability drop.

Curves may be drawn overall or stratified by an exposure or confounder. Axis scaling is important when the event is rare, because a default zero-to-one probability axis can make meaningful differences near one visually disappear.

2266.sourceSearchName: survival data selection bias survival data selection bias
2266.title: Survival Data Selection Bias
2266.heading: Document

2267.sourceSearchName: survival data selection bias survival data selection bias
2267.title: Survival Data Selection Bias
2267.heading: Survival Data Selection Bias
2267.content:
Survival data selection bias arises when eligibility for time-to-event analysis depends on having a recorded event time or follow-up measurement, and that availability differs systematically across participants. Removing most event-positive records can leave a highly unrepresentative analytic sample.

A missingness audit should quantify the loss before modeling. Imputing nearly all event times would substitute assumptions for evidence, so a demonstrative analysis may proceed only with an explicit warning while a substantive study may need a different outcome or dataset.

2268.sourceSearchName: survival data selection bias survival data selection bias
2268.title: Survival Data Selection Bias
2268.heading: References

2270.title: Survival Analysis
2270.heading: Survival Analysis
2270.content:
Survival analysis studies whether and when an event occurs while accounting for observations whose event time is not fully observed. Each record combines an event indicator with a time-to-event or censoring time.

The method can describe survival curves, compare groups, or estimate adjusted hazard or time relationships. It is only as credible as the event timing and observation window; uncertain diagnosis dates can make a simpler binary-outcome analysis more defensible.

2273.title: Surrogate Variable Analysis
2273.heading: Surrogate Variable Analysis
2273.content:
Surrogate variable analysis estimates latent sources of unwanted variation while protecting the modeled outcome of interest. It iteratively weights features according to whether they are associated with hidden structure but not with the biological contrast, then estimates surrogate factors from the weighted data.

The resulting variables enter the model beside the biological predictor. This outcome-aware construction reduces the risk of deleting the target signal when batch labels are incomplete or unknown.

2276.title: Surplus Variable
2276.heading: Surplus Variable
2276.content:
A surplus variable converts a greater-than-or-equal constraint into an equality by subtracting a nonnegative quantity: $a^Tx-s=b$.

The surplus measures how far the left side exceeds the required minimum. Because its column does not automatically provide an identity basis, an [[Artificial Variable]] may also be needed.

2279.title: Surjective Function
2279.heading: Surjective Function
2279.content:
A surjective function reaches every element of its codomain. Its image therefore equals the codomain.

For a surjective homomorphism, the first isomorphism theorem presents the target as a quotient of the source by the kernel.

Surjectivity depends on the declared codomain: the same assignment may be onto one codomain but not a larger one. Every codomain element must have at least one preimage.

2281.sourceSearchName: surface to surface radiation surface to surface radiation
2281.title: Surface-to-Surface Radiation
2281.heading: Document

2282.sourceSearchName: surface to surface radiation surface to surface radiation
2282.title: Surface-to-Surface Radiation
2282.heading: Surface-to-Surface Radiation
2282.content:
Surface-to-surface radiation models exchange among boundaries separated by a transparent or partially participating medium. Each surface emits according to its temperature and emissivity and receives energy from other surfaces according to their [[Radiative View Factor|view factors]].

The model must distinguish exterior surfaces facing an ambient from enclosed surfaces that see one another. Opacity, diffuse or specular behavior, wavelength dependence, and shadowing determine whether a simple ambient-radiation condition is adequate or full enclosure exchange is needed.

2283.title: Surface-to-Surface Radiation

2284.title: Surface Radiation Coupling
2284.heading: Document

2285.sourceSearchName: surface radiation coupling surface radiation coupling
2285.title: Surface Radiation Coupling
2285.heading: Surface Radiation Coupling
2285.content:
Surface radiation coupling adds radiative heat flux to the boundary energy balance of a solid or solid-fluid thermal model. The same temperature field that results from conduction and convection determines emission, while absorbed radiation changes that field in return.

Exterior boundaries may exchange with an ambient, and mutually visible interior boundaries may require [[Surface-to-Surface Radiation|radiosity and view factors]]. Shared dependent variables and consistent emissivity definitions prevent separate physics interfaces from applying contradictory temperatures.

2288.sourceSearchName: surface work function surface work function
2288.title: Surface Work Function
2288.heading: Surface Work Function
2288.content: Work function is the energy required for an electron inside a solid to escape the attractive barrier at its surface. The source gives different values for different metals and uses it to explain why heating an emitter releases only some electrons. Together with temperature, it controls [[Thermionic Emission]] rate; emitter and collector work functions also affect the voltage of a [[Thermionic Generator]].

2289.sourceSearchName: surface work function surface work function

2290.title: Surface Emissivity and Absorptivity

2291.sourceSearchName: surface emissivity and absorptivity surface emissivity and absorptivity
2291.title: Surface Emissivity and Absorptivity
2291.heading: Surface Emissivity and Absorptivity
2291.content:
Emissivity measures how effectively a real surface emits radiation relative to an ideal black body, with values between zero and one. Absorptivity describes the fraction of incident radiation absorbed rather than reflected or transmitted.

Both properties depend on surface condition and may depend on wavelength, direction, and temperature. They influence [[Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Law|radiative exchange]] and infrared temperature measurement, so coatings, oxidation, or an assumed gray-surface approximation can materially change a thermal result.

2294.title: Supra-Adjacency Matrix
2294.heading: Supra-Adjacency Matrix
2294.content:
A supra-adjacency matrix represents an entire multilayer network as a block matrix. Diagonal blocks contain each layer's [[Adjacency Matrix]], while off-diagonal blocks encode [[Interlayer Edge|interlayer edges]].

This form permits matrix, spectral, walk, and path methods to be extended from single graphs. The resulting super-network may still behave differently from an aggregation that merges all copies of a node.

2297.sourceSearchName: suppression of parentheses suppression of parentheses
2297.title: Suppression of Parentheses
2297.heading: Suppression of Parentheses
2297.content:
Suppression of parentheses removes grouping symbols while preserving the value of an expression. A plus sign before a group leaves its terms unchanged, while a minus sign negates each term:

$$-(a+b)=-a-b,$$

$$-(a-b)=-a+b.$$

More generally, a factor outside a group is distributed to every internal term. After parentheses are removed, [[Combining Like Terms]] can simplify the result. Parentheses are not redundant when they determine the base of a power or distinguish a product from a sum.

2298.sourceSearchName: suppression of parentheses suppression of parentheses
2298.title: Suppression of Parentheses
2298.heading: References

2299.title: Sum of Cubes Identity
2299.heading: Document

2300.sourceSearchName: sum of cubes identity sum of cubes identity
2300.title: Sum of Cubes Identity
2300.heading: Sum of Cubes Identity
2300.content:
The sum of cubes identity factors two cubes as

$$a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2).$$

The sign in the linear factor matches the sum, while the middle term of the quadratic factor has the opposite sign. Expansion verifies that the mixed cubic terms cancel.

The identity applies whenever both terms are recognizable cubes, including coefficients and variable powers. It can be combined with other methods; for example, (x^6-1) first becomes a difference of squares and then its cubic factors can be decomposed separately.

2301.sourceSearchName: sum of cubes identity sum of cubes identity
2301.title: Sum of Cubes Identity

2303.title: Suppressing Chroma Spill
2303.heading: Suppressing Chroma Spill
2303.content: Light reflected from a blue or green screen can tint the subject, especially at its edges. Removing the screen in the alpha does not automatically remove this contamination from RGB. The book's blue-screen stereo example uses a hue correction to isolate and reduce blue spill after the initial key, then uses the alpha to retrieve the performer from original footage. Spill correction is therefore a color operation coordinated with, but separate from, [[Retaining Pristine RGB During Keying]].
